guide.title: The Old White: Golf in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia
guide.intro: Golf Digest's 2025-'26 ranking of the best golf courses in West Virginia — the page states, "Below you'll find our 2025-'26 ranking of the Best Golf Courses in West Virginia" — puts The Greenbrier: Old White third, rated 4.5 by 14 panelists and labelled "Public," carrying the badges "100 Greatest Public" and "Best In State." It is the highest-ranked publicly accessible course on that list. The two entries above it are labelled "Private," and their operators say the same thing in their own words: Pikewood National Golf Club, in Morgantown, writes that "The golf course and Club facilities are only available to Members and their guests. A Member must accompany guests while on Club grounds," and Pete Dye Golf Club, in Bridgeport, answers its own FAQ heading "Is Pete Dye Golf Club open to the public?" with "Pete Dye Golf Club is a private golf course and membership is required to play." The Old White is one of the courses at The Greenbrier, 101 Main Street West, White Sulphur Springs, in Greenbrier County. Charles Blair Macdonald and Seth Raynor built it in 1914. It held the same rank and the same "Public" label in the previous edition of the ranking. A second Greenbrier course, The Meadows, is ninth on the same list and also labelled "Public"; it is this guide's second round.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The Greenbrier's postal address is 101 Main Street West, White Sulphur Springs, WV 24986, and the resort's own interactive map tags the Old White at 37.787702629526365, -80.3141898324812. The US Census geocoder returns Greenbrier County for that point, county subdivision "Eastern district," and no Incorporated Place at all. That absence is meaningful rather than a glitch: the same geocoder returns "White Sulphur Springs city" for an address on the town's own Main Street, 0.6 miles away, and "Charleston city" for Charleston. The resort's own postal address geocodes the same way as the map pin — Greenbrier County, Eastern district, no place. The golf courses lie outside the White Sulphur Springs city limits and carry the town as a postal address.

The airport is Greenbrier Valley Airport (LWB), 584 Airport Road, Lewisburg, WV 24901, which describes its own position: "Located 3 miles north of the Lewisburg exit off I-64 on North U.S. 219, Greenbrier Valley Airport (LWB) is the closest major airport to The Greenbrier, The Homestead and Snowshoe Mountain Resort." On air service it states: "Sky West Airlines offers non-stop service to Charlotte and Chicago and connections through American Airlines to destinations across the US." The airport publishes at mylwb.com; the older gvairport.com address redirects there. From the terminal to the course is 12.5 road miles, by Airport Road, Seneca Trail North (US 219), North Jefferson Street (US 219), I-64, Harts Run Road (CR 60/14) and US 60.

Lewisburg, also in Greenbrier County, lies west along US 60. Measured from The Historic General Lewis Inn on East Washington Street to the course, the road distance is 8.62 miles, by East Washington Street (US 60) and Midland Trail East (US 60); measured the other way, from the course back to the inn by West Main Street (US 60), it is 9.28 miles. The route is asymmetric, so the direction is worth stating.

Parking, in the resort's own words: "Complimentary self-parking is available for guests at The Greenbrier. Valet parking is also available for a $35 per night fee."

sections.heading: The Old White
sections.body:
The resort's golf-history page: "Originally designed and constructed by Charles Blair Macdonald and Seth Raynor in 1914, The Old White has stood the test of time and is still considered one of the finest courses in the United States more than 100 years later." The course page gives the name's origin — it "was named for the well-known Old White Hotel, which stood on the resort grounds from 1858 through 1922" — and names the template holes: "Charles Blair Macdonald, the father of American golf course design, graced The Old White with an architectural homage to some of Europe's most iconic greens. Its 8th hole was styled after the 'Redan' at North Berwick, the 13th after the 'Alps' at Prestwick, and the 15th after the 'Eden' at St. Andrews."

Golf Digest's own entry for the course credits two separate projects to two different architects, and they are easy to collapse into one: "C.B. Macdonald's early American design of the Old White at The Greenbrier was always respected, especially after Lester George's 2007 restoration re-established such things as a Principal's Nose bunker and Dragon's Teeth mounds. Golf Digest panelists rediscovered its pleasures and ranked it the Best New Public Remodel of 2007. Soon, owner Jim Justice began sponsoring an annual PGA Tour event. Then came devastating floods in July 2016, which claimed lives and destroyed several Old White holes. Another architect, Keith Foster, supervised a total rebuild of the famed course in less than 12 months, in time for the following year's PGA Tour event. As a result, The Old White was named Golf Digest's Best New Remodel again in 2017." The resort's own account of the same work is shorter: "The course saw a major restoration project after a catastrophic weather event in 2016. The Old White received new fairways, new bunkers, and new green complexes, and changes were made to return the course as close as possible to its original design."

Maintenance, from the course page: "Aeration Schedule: May 4 – May 8, 2026 | August 31 – September 4, 2026." On season, the Old White rate card prices all twelve months and contains no "Course Closed" cell — unlike the Meadows card, which uses that exact phrase. The one exception is the nine-hole option, marked "Not Available" from May 1 to October 25. Beyond that single aeration line the resort publishes no course-conditions page and no blackout notice, which is recorded here as an absence rather than as a guarantee. No 2026 event at the resort appears on the LIV Golf schedule, whose twelve listed 2026 stops contain no West Virginia entry, and the resort's press page announces no 2026 tournament and no closure.

Of the competitive record, the course page says only: "This classic design has attracted the PGA TOUR and LIV Golf, among others, to host major events on this iconic tract."

The National Park Service's list of National Historic Landmarks, under the heading "West Virginia (17)," carries "The Greenbrier — 06/21/90 — White Sulphur Springs, Greenbrier County, WV." Read that precisely: the designation of 21 June 1990 is for the resort, and the NPS entry names no golf course. Whether the Old White's ground falls inside the designated boundary is not established, and this guide does not claim it.

sections.heading: Playing it without a room
sections.body:
Golf Digest labels the Old White "Public," and the operator's own pages agree with the label — not by opening the course to all comers, and not by gating it behind exclusion, but by pricing it in tiers. The resort's rate page for the Old White publishes two green-fee columns side by side, headed exactly "Registered Guests" and "Non-Registered." A published non-guest price is the operator's own statement that a player who is not booked into the resort may play. The identical two-column structure appears on the rate pages for The Meadows and for The Greenbrier Course, so the tier is a standing structure of the golf operation rather than an artefact of one page.

Membership is not the gate either. The Greenbrier's Golf and Tennis Club membership page describes both of its tiers as a discount off the published green fee rather than as permission to play, and a discount off a green fee presupposes a green fee payable by someone who is not a member. Eight operator pages were read for exclusion language — the golf landing page, the Old White course and rates pages, the Meadows course and rates pages, the resort policies page, the memberships page and the tee-time page. The phrases "members only," "resort guests only," "hotel guests only," "not open to the public," "must be a guest," "day pass" and "day visitor" appear zero times across all eight. The resort policies page publishes no day-visitor gate fee and no property-access charge. So: a traveller with no accommodation booked and no membership can request a tee time at a published non-guest rate.

Two artefacts carry the request path. The golf landing page and the Old White course page both print "To Request a Tee Time Please Call" above +1 844-837-2466. And the resort's own sitemap lists https://www.greenbrier.com/golf/book-a-tee-time/, which serves a live form headed "Request A Tee Time." Its Golf Course selector offers The Old White, The Greenbrier, The Meadows and The Ashford Short Course; it asks for date of play, preferred time and players in the group; and its required question, "Do you have an accommodation booked?", offers Yes and No. The form's own copy reads: "To secure a tee time at a golf course, golf enthusiasts can typically submit a request or reservation, allowing them to claim a coveted spot on the picturesque fairways, or give us a call at +1 844-837-2466." That page is orphaned from the golf section — no golf page links to it, and it is reachable only through the sitemap or site search.

The honest shape of the claim, then. The form is a request, not a tee sheet: it shows no availability, quotes no price, issues no confirmation and takes no payment, and no third-party tee-sheet host — foreUp, GolfNow, Supreme Golf, Chronogolf, teeoff — appears on any Greenbrier golf page. Access here is evidenced by published operator policy: a non-guest price column, a membership that sells a discount rather than a right, no exclusion language anywhere, and an intake form built to accept a request from a player with no room booked. It is not evidenced by a booking that was executed and watched, and it is weaker on that axis than a course whose tee sheet can be driven. Two questions the resort answers nowhere, and this guide will not answer for it: whether Non-Registered tee times are capped or released only inside a window, and whether they sit behind registered guests on a space-available basis.

On price, this guide publishes no green fee. The Old White rate page carries no dated qualifier of any kind: no season year, no "effective" line, and no year attached to any of its six date ranges, which are month-and-day only. The only two years anywhere in the page's text are a footer copyright and a sentence about a different course. A fee publishes here only with the operator's own dated qualifier, and The Greenbrier supplies none — that is the rule working, not a gap. What the page does state about its rates is what they exclude: "Please note that taxes and the Historic Preservation Fund are not included in the course rates."

sections.heading: The weekend around the course
sections.body:
The basecamp is the resort itself. Its room types, in its own descriptions: Traditional Rooms, 250 square feet for two to four people — "a collection of intimate sanctuaries that feel every bit home-away-from-home as they do luxury hotel"; Superior Rooms, 400 square feet, "offering ample space to unwind after a day of exploring the resort grounds"; Deluxe Rooms, also 400 square feet, "featuring an enhanced layout, understated furnishings, and a subdued color palette unique from other Greenbrier accommodations"; Draper Suites, 600 square feet for four to six, "The Greenbrier's largest single room" and "a vibrant homage to the legendary Dorothy Draper"; and West Virginia Suites, 1300 square feet — "Originally built to conceal the construction of the Cold War fallout shelter underneath The Greenbrier, staying in one of these suites means staying in a piece of American history."

The lodging-side charges the resort publishes are a Daily Resort Fee of $49.00 per room, per night, which it states includes Morning Coffee Service, Afternoon Tea and Concert, Nightly Movies in the Theatre, Historical Tours & Presentations, Fitness Equipment, Children's VIP Bags, Resort-Wide Wireless Internet, use of the indoor and outdoor pools, a Champagne Toast in The Casino Club (Tuesday through Saturday), On-Property Transportation, Hiking & Meditation Trails and the Springhouse Entertainer Cabaret; "West Virginia State Taxes: 6% sales tax & 3% occupancy tax"; and the Historic Preservation Fund at 9.75%. One line from the same page is worth carrying to the first tee: "Pets are not permitted in the restaurants or food-serving areas, in the pools or on the golf courses."

Three of the resort's dining rooms sit at the golf. Sam Snead's — "With stunning views of the courses, this relaxed, seasonal dining destination at The Golf Club offers an à la carte menu featuring wood-fired favorites." Slammin' Sammy's — "Overlooking our picturesque golf courses, our elevated sports bar is the perfect place to watch the game or play shuffleboard. Open seasonally." And the Ryder Cup Snack Bar — "Stop by our fully stocked snack bar for light bites, beverages, and grab-and-golf snacks before, during, and after your round." Both Sam Snead's and Slammin' Sammy's are marked seasonal in the resort's own copy, as are Tree Tops Café and Springhouse Smoothies. What the source establishes is that these rooms exist and what they serve; none of them says whether any given room is serving this week, so this guide does not say so either.

Away from the courses the resort's dining page names Prime 44 West, a steak house "honoring NBA legend and West Virginia native Jerry West"; Draper's Café, for "the soulful flavors of the South and beloved Dorothy Draper recipes"; The Forum, for "Hand-tossed Neapolitan pizza, handpicked tomatoes from our garden, and fresh burrata"; The Pizza Shoppe, which "uses one of two Anthracite coal-fired ovens in West Virginia"; and the Main Dining Room, Lobby Bar, JJ's Sports Lounge, Café Carleton and The Greenbrier Gourmet & Coffee Bar. Sam Snead himself is the through-line at the golf restaurants: the resort records that he "was first hired as the Assistant Golf Professional at The Greenbrier in 1936 before serving as our resort's Golf Professional from 1946 through 1974," and was "rehired as the Golf Professional Emeritus in 1993 and remained in that position until his death in 2002."

Off the property, in Lewisburg: The Historic General Lewis Inn & Restaurant, 1236 Washington Street East. In its own words it is "comprised of 23 luxurious rooms and suites in a restored 1834 and 1928 historic building. The East wing is an 1834 historic residence, and the West wing was built onto the residence and made into a hotel in the 1920s." It was "named after a prominent general in the French & Indian War." On the food: "We aim to please with down-to-earth Southern cooking. Think Grandma's cooking, but healthier and with the finest of ingredients from our local farms and gardens." There is also "the Thistle Lounge to relax and enjoy one of our unique craft cocktails." The Census geocoder places that address in Greenbrier County, Incorporated Place "Lewisburg city."

sections.heading: Day two: The Meadows
sections.body:
The second course is The Greenbrier: Meadows, ninth on the same Golf Digest 2025-'26 list and also labelled "Public." It is 1.3 road miles from the Old White, at the same resort, on the same access terms: its rate page publishes the same "Registered Guest" and "Non-Registered" columns, and it appears in the same "Request A Tee Time" course selector. Its rate page has the same defect as the Old White's — no dated qualifier, only a footer copyright — so no fee for it is published here either.

The resort's history of it: "The Meadows Course began as a 9-hole course named Lakeside. Designed by Alexander H. Findlay, it opened for play in 1911. In 1923, Seth Raynor redesigned the course while he was on the property, updating The Old White and building the original Greenbrier Course. In 1962, Lakeside was expanded to an 18-hole routing by architect Dick Wilson, who used dirt excavated during the construction of The Bunker to expand the course. Years later, in 1999, Bob Cupp once again redesigned the golf course, at which point it officially became known as The Meadows." On the same flood that took out the Old White: "After the force of nature left its mark on this course in a 2016 flood, The Meadows underwent a complete restoration. In the summer of 2017, it emerged anew with dynamic green complexes, breathtaking mountain vistas, and our signature stacked sod bunkers throughout the course."

Unlike the Old White, The Meadows closes for part of the year, and the operator says so in the rate table itself. The literal cell value "Course Closed" appears for January 1 – March 26 in every column, and again in winter: November 30 – December 31 in the Registered Guest rows and in the Non-Registered nine-hole row, but November 30 – December 30 in the Non-Registered 18-hole row. The resort's own table disagrees with itself by one day there; both values are reproduced as printed. Aeration, from the course page: "Aeration Schedule: June 29 – July 3, 2026 | October 28 – November 5, 2026."

One alternative, if the second round is to be played at a different facility rather than a different course: The Resort At Glade Springs: Cobb, fifth on the same list and labelled "Public," in Daniels, Raleigh County. It is 58.0 road miles from the Old White by West Main Street (US 60), CR 60/14, I-64, Grandview Road (CR 9), Ritter Drive (US 19; WV 3), Lake Drive, Allenwood Lane and Manor House Drive, and 51.6 road miles from Greenbrier Valley Airport. Its rate table is headed "2026 RATE CARD" in the operator's own capitals and its first row is labelled "Public Guest" — a dated qualifier of exactly the kind The Greenbrier's pages lack. Booking there is by telephone: every course tile reads "Call for Tee Time." It is an alternative, not this guide's second course.

faq.question: Can I play the Old White without staying at The Greenbrier?
faq.answer: The operator's own rate page publishes two green-fee columns, "Registered Guests" and "Non-Registered" — a published price for a player who is not booked into the resort. Memberships are described on the resort's own membership page as a discount off the green fee rather than as permission to play, and no membership, sponsor, host, pass or day-visitor requirement appears on any of the eight Greenbrier pages read for this guide. The resort's "Request A Tee Time" form makes the same point from the other side: its required question "Do you have an accommodation booked?" offers Yes and No.

faq.question: How do I book a tee time?
faq.answer: Two paths, both requests rather than reservations. The golf landing page and the Old White course page print "To Request a Tee Time Please Call" above +1 844-837-2466. And https://www.greenbrier.com/golf/book-a-tee-time/, listed in the resort's own sitemap but linked from no golf page, serves a form headed "Request A Tee Time" whose course selector includes The Old White. Neither shows availability, quotes a price, issues a confirmation or takes payment, so no booking behaviour was observed for this guide — the access claim rests on published operator policy.

faq.question: What does a round cost?
faq.answer: This guide publishes no green fee for the Old White or The Meadows. Both rate pages carry no dated qualifier: no season year, no "effective" line, and no year on any of the date ranges, which are month-and-day only. A fee publishes here only with the operator's own dated qualifier. The page does state that "taxes and the Historic Preservation Fund are not included in the course rates," and the resort's policies page puts the Historic Preservation Fund at 9.75% and West Virginia taxes at 6% sales and 3% occupancy.

faq.question: Is the Old White open in winter?
faq.answer: The Old White rate card prices all twelve months and contains no "Course Closed" cell; the nine-hole option is the exception, marked "Not Available" from May 1 to October 25. The Meadows is the course with stated winter closures — "Course Closed" for January 1 – March 26 and again from November 30 to the end of December. The resort publishes no course-conditions page, so the aeration dates and the rate table are the whole of what it says about season.

faq.question: When is the course aerated?
faq.answer: The Old White course page states: "Aeration Schedule: May 4 – May 8, 2026 | August 31 – September 4, 2026." The Meadows course page states: "Aeration Schedule: June 29 – July 3, 2026 | October 28 – November 5, 2026."

faq.question: Where exactly is the course?
faq.answer: At The Greenbrier, 101 Main Street West, White Sulphur Springs, WV 24986. The US Census geocoder returns Greenbrier County for the resort's own map coordinate for the Old White, county subdivision "Eastern district," and no Incorporated Place — the property sits outside the White Sulphur Springs city limits and carries the town as a postal address. Greenbrier Valley Airport (LWB) is 12.5 road miles away by US 219, I-64, Harts Run Road (CR 60/14) and US 60.

faq.question: Is the golf course a National Historic Landmark?
faq.answer: The National Park Service lists "The Greenbrier — 06/21/90 — White Sulphur Springs, Greenbrier County, WV" among West Virginia's National Historic Landmarks. The designation names the resort, not a golf course, and whether the Old White's ground falls inside the designated boundary is not established. This guide therefore makes no landmark claim about the course itself.

places.name: The Old White
places.summary: Third on Golf Digest's 2025-'26 ranking of the best golf courses in West Virginia, rated 4.5 by 14 panelists and labelled "Public" with the badges "100 Greatest Public" and "Best In State" — the highest-ranked publicly accessible course in the state on that list. Charles Blair Macdonald and Seth Raynor built it at The Greenbrier in 1914; its 8th hole is styled after the "Redan" at North Berwick, the 13th after the "Alps" at Prestwick and the 15th after the "Eden" at St. Andrews. Lester George restored it in 2007 and Keith Foster rebuilt it after the July 2016 floods. The resort prices it in two published tiers, "Registered Guests" and "Non-Registered."

places.name: The Greenbrier: Meadows
places.summary: Ninth on the same Golf Digest 2025-'26 West Virginia ranking and also labelled "Public," 1.3 road miles from the Old White at the same resort and on the same published "Registered Guest" and "Non-Registered" rate tiers. It began as the 9-hole Lakeside, designed by Alexander H. Findlay and opened for play in 1911, was redesigned by Seth Raynor in 1923, expanded to 18 holes by Dick Wilson in 1962 and redesigned by Bob Cupp in 1999, when it took its present name. Its rate table marks "Course Closed" for January 1 – March 26 and for the turn of the year.

places.name: The Greenbrier
places.summary: The resort that owns the Old White, at 101 Main Street West. Its published room types run Traditional (250 sq ft), Superior and Deluxe (400 sq ft), Draper Suites (600 sq ft) and West Virginia Suites (1300 sq ft), the last "originally built to conceal the construction of the Cold War fallout shelter underneath The Greenbrier." A Daily Resort Fee of $49.00 per room, per night covers coffee service, afternoon tea, movies, historical tours, the pools, on-property transportation and the hiking trails; West Virginia taxes run 6% sales and 3% occupancy, and the Historic Preservation Fund is 9.75%. Self-parking is complimentary for guests; valet is $35 per night. The National Park Service lists The Greenbrier as a National Historic Landmark designated 06/21/90.

places.name: The Historic General Lewis Inn & Restaurant
places.summary: 1236 Washington Street East, Lewisburg, 8.62 road miles from the Old White by US 60. In its own words, "comprised of 23 luxurious rooms and suites in a restored 1834 and 1928 historic building. The East wing is an 1834 historic residence, and the West wing was built onto the residence and made into a hotel in the 1920s." Its dining room serves "down-to-earth Southern cooking" and there is a Thistle Lounge for cocktails. The Census geocoder places the address in Greenbrier County, Incorporated Place "Lewisburg city."

places.name: Sam Snead's
places.summary: The Greenbrier's dining room at The Golf Club, named for the professional the resort hired as an assistant in 1936 and kept as Golf Professional from 1946 through 1974. The resort's description: "With stunning views of the courses, this relaxed, seasonal dining destination at The Golf Club offers an à la carte menu featuring wood-fired favorites." Marked seasonal in the operator's own copy.

places.name: Slammin' Sammy's
places.summary: The resort's sports bar at the golf courses: "Overlooking our picturesque golf courses, our elevated sports bar is the perfect place to watch the game or play shuffleboard. Open seasonally."

places.name: Ryder Cup Snack Bar
places.summary: The Greenbrier's snack bar for the golf: "Stop by our fully stocked snack bar for light bites, beverages, and grab-and-golf snacks before, during, and after your round."

places.name: Prime 44 West
places.summary: The resort's steak house: "Feast on the finest aged beef and fresh seafood at our classic steak house honoring NBA legend and West Virginia native Jerry West." JJ's Sports Lounge sits beneath it.

places.name: Draper's Café
places.summary: Named for the resort's decorator Dorothy Draper: "Savor the soulful flavors of the South and beloved Dorothy Draper recipes in a uniquely vibrant and colorful atmosphere."

places.name: The Pizza Shoppe
places.summary: One of the resort's dining rooms, and the operator makes one claim for it: "The Pizza Shoppe uses one of two Anthracite coal-fired ovens in West Virginia."
